title: Sable and the Grumpy Moss-Hare
markdown:
In the hidden highlands, waterfalls whispered and stairs were cut into rock-bone. Ravens kept old opinions. Elf Sable watched the world the way some people watch clocks: a tail-twitch, a web’s tremble, all of it filed.

The Whispering Market swirled around him—creatures, wonders, the problem of a familiar. Choices fluttered and squawked. He wanted quiet, not a résumé.

Lyra Meadowlight’s harp chimed, moonlight-on-water voice. “Sable, brave elf, sung by bards, deeds across the glades—”

He smoothed his moss-green tunic. “I want a squirrel that doesn’t shed much. Heroic sounds like a lot.” A vendor sold pebbles that chirped without inspiration. A thumb-sized sliver of shadow flickered behind a turnip. In damp moss lounged Bartholomew, a moss-hare bored by everything including Sable: velvet-leaf ears, a nose that suspected cheer.

“If you’re going to be mysterious,” rumbled Wizard Quill, beard a wispy cloud, eyes storing jokes, “be on time. My tea is getting cold.”

“I am choosing a companion. This is delightful chaos.” A gnome haggled with a griffin over moonstones. Furry shoppers interrogated mushrooms.

Lyra swelled toward destiny and partnerships. Sable groaned. “I need a satchel carried. Berries found. Not a dragon I haven’t met. If I met one I would offer a biscuit and hope.” Bartholomew yawned, slow, a walking patch of moss that regretted the career. Grump: loyalty, or nap?

Pixies giggled through in rainbow blur. Berries, trinkets, a baker’s hat flew. Sable dodged without wobble. Bartholomew was already asleep, snores a soft argument against noise. He had not flinched.

Quill’s chuckle was pebbles. He did not lecture. He drank the tea that had been getting cold.

Sable looked at the pebble’s loop, the hiding wisp, the hare whose snores were dry leaves. Bartholomew was unimpressed. He was there. When Lyra mentioned glory he snored louder. Not seeking legend. Seeking sleep.

Lyra challenged: boldest, wisest, destiny’s hand, a familiar worthy of song. Something competitive, usually reserved for archery, lit. Sable walked to the moss bed.

“Five minutes awake. One grumpy grunt. Interview.”

An ear twitched. One dull green eye. A huff like old bellows.

“A roar, practically. Stoic.”

He scooped. Bartholomew grumbled and snuggled deeper into the elbow. Lyra’s song paused; surprise did a small, honest thing on her face. Heroes, she had assumed. He had hired a nap.

They left on stone paths. Under a mighty bridge, glow-worms pulsed in damp moss, a silent underside of stars on the gorge. Quill, leisurely on an outcrop, nodded and did not explain the moment. Sable looked at the hare in the satchel, contented snuffles, and felt the pride of a choice made with his own eyes. Lyra, from a cliff, found a quieter tune without being asked. The highland kept its hidden lamps. Sable kept Bartholomew, who kept being late for glory and on time for tea.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing fantasy story for middle-grade readers
